name: Grace Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Grace, and thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party. What you say here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: So I'm an excavator operator, junior, at a big lithium mine, the metal that goes in car batteries. I'm in a 120-tonne digger in the pit, loading ore into the haul trucks, three or four buckets a truck. I came from a warehouse job two years ago because the money was better, and I'm still on the training rate, so it's better but not by as much as people assume. My day is a pre-start check, a safety talk, then loading trucks till my hands ache.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when I get a good rhythm, bucket, swing, dump, swing back, and the truck drivers stop waiting on me. Hardest part is the days I don't, when my trainer Priya gets on the radio and says 'Grace, the trucks are queuing.' Money's the other hard part. I've got a car loan and about two thousand on a credit card from when I moved out here, and my partner Sam stacks shelves at the supermarket, so the card doesn't really go down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like 'well, that was a lot of fuss for a better spellcheck.' At work I'd just mention it at lunch. I'm not much of a poster online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved. Lithium's busy, everyone wants batteries, so if nothing changes with AI I've got years of work. It gives me time to get good at this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally attack the credit card. I've got a spreadsheet, Sam laughs at it, I'd put an extra fifty a fortnight on it until it's gone. And I'd ask Priya to sign me off on the bigger digger by the end of next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a spreadsheet. Do you use AI tools for that kind of thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I got one of the chat apps to help me set the spreadsheet up, and to rewrite my CV when I applied here. I wouldn't trust it with anything at work, but for boring stuff it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'getting good at this' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loading a truck in three buckets instead of four, every time. Not getting called on the radio. And one day being the person a new trainee gets put with, like Priya was for me.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of fuss for a better spellcheck and mention it at lunch. I'm not much of a poster online.
S0.think: I think I'd be relieved, because lithium is busy and a quiet AI world gives me years of work. It gives me time to get good at this.
S0.do: Puts an extra fifty a fortnight on the credit card, tracked in her spreadsheet, until it's cleared. Asks her trainer to sign her off on the bigger excavator by the end of next year.
S0.feel: Mostly calm, maybe a little smug.
S0.quote: Well, that was a lot of fuss for a better spellcheck.
S0.fieldNote: She's organised and goal-driven, with a spreadsheet for her debt and a clear picture of what being good at her job means. She uses AI for personal admin but keeps it out of work. Lithium demand makes her feel the industry itself is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change things, so people should pay attention and not bury their heads. I'd probably say that to my mum on the phone, she worries about me out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think diggers are further down the list than trucks. Loading's fiddly, the rock is never the same twice. But the trucks I load might drive themselves, and then the whole pit runs differently. I'd want to know where I fit in that before someone else decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor straight out what the automation plan is, and I'd watch who gets moved where in the first few months. If people who did the remote training kept their jobs, I'd sign up. I'd keep paying the card down and stop the takeaway on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a weather forecast with a storm somewhere out west.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see who keeps their jobs before signing up. Why not sign up straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because two years ago I took a forklift course on the side and three months later the warehouse got automatic forklifts. I don't want to train for the thing that's about to go. Better to see which way the cat jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jake, one of the truck drivers who waits on me. He's my age, he's got a baby on the way. If the trucks go self-driving first, it's him before me, and I'd feel awful being glad about that.

S1.say: I'd say things are going to change and people should pay attention rather than bury their heads. I'd tell my mum that on the phone.
S1.think: I think diggers are further down the list than trucks because loading is fiddly, but self-driving trucks would change how the whole pit runs. I want to know where I fit before someone else decides.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor directly about the automation plan and watches who gets moved where for a few months. Signs up for remote training once it's clearly protecting jobs, keeps paying down the card and stops Friday takeaway.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm forecast somewhere out west.
S1.quote: I don't want to train for the thing that's about to go.
S1.fieldNote: She's been burned before: a forklift course just before her warehouse automated its forklifts. That's why she waits to see what works. She separated her own odds from a truck driver's and felt guilty about being relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal and the government and companies need a proper plan, fast. Not a scare campaign, a plan. I'd probably share some practical stuff, like where to get help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I've got a car loan, a credit card and a junior ticket. I'd be twenty-nine starting from zero, again, and this time there'd be no warehouse to go back to either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't rent, food or the car. I'd ask Sam to pick up any extra hours and I'd look for any job the robots haven't reached yet, even if it pays less, maybe in the town's aged care or the council. If it all fell over I'd go on support and we'd probably move back near my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but trying to make a list about it, which is how I deal with scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam would pick up extra hours. Is his job safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, worse probably. Supermarkets are already testing robots for shelves. I said it because it's the only extra money I can think of. We'd both be on thin ice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go on the list first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Number one, call the car loan people before I miss a payment, not after. Number two, cancel the phone upgrade I've been planning. Number three, ask Mum if the spare room is free. It's a short list, which is the scary bit.

S2.say: I'd say it's a big deal and government and companies need a proper plan quickly, not a scare campaign. I'd share practical information about where to get help.
S2.think: I think with a car loan, a credit card and a junior ticket I'd be starting from zero at twenty-nine. This time there'd be no warehouse to go back to.
S2.do: Cuts every expense except rent, food and the car in the first month and calls the car lender before missing a payment. Looks for any work robots haven't reached, such as aged care, and falls back on support and her mother's spare room if that fails.
S2.feel: Scared, and coping by making lists.
S2.quote: It's a short list, which is the scary bit.
S2.fieldNote: Her coping style is to turn fear into a numbered list, and the list's shortness is what frightens her. She quickly admitted her partner's supermarket job was even more exposed. She'd act early on the debt, which fits her careful habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some years, so let's use them properly. Companies should train people and the government should help with the bills while we do it. Pretty middle of the road, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to clear my debts and get one solid skill. Not enough to feel safe. I'd be thirty-two, which isn't old, but I don't want to start over at thirty-two with a credit card still open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, clear the card, then save a month of expenses, which I've never had. Once the first remote digger jobs showed up, probably year two, I'd go for them. I'd also look at a maintenance course, because someone has to fix the machines, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can use. It's a timeline. I like timelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'at least for a while' about fixing machines. Do you think that lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. Maybe the robots fix the robots by 2031, I honestly don't know. I'd pick it because it buys me a few years, and a few years is what I need to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had one month of savings, what would that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep, probably. Right now a broken tyre is a crisis. With a month I could say no to a bad shift swap or take a course without panicking. It sounds small but I've never had it.

S3.say: I'd say we have some years and should use them, with companies training people and government helping with bills meanwhile. I know that's pretty middle of the road.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to clear my debts and get one solid skill, but not enough to feel safe. I don't want to start over at thirty-two with a credit card still open.
S3.do: Clears the credit card in the first year and builds a month of savings for the first time. Goes for remote excavator jobs once they appear, probably in year two, and looks at a maintenance course.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a timeline.
S3.quote: Right now a broken tyre is a crisis.
S3.fieldNote: She turns the five years into a plan almost instantly, because timelines suit her. A single month of savings would change her life more than she expected to admit. She's realistic that maintenance work only buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people start now, and that's on all of us: workers, bosses and government. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'm actually okay with. I'd have time to get good at this job, get debt free, and change track around thirty-two or so with savings behind me. That's a normal career change, people do that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the debt, then the savings, then sign up for a two-year technical diploma at night, maybe in electrical or automation, once I see which one the mine is hiring for. Sam and I would probably hold off on buying a place until I knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like 'okay, homework' than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on buying a place. Was that coming soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not soon, more like a dream for my thirties. A little house with a shed in a town with a real supermarket. I'd still want it. I'd just want to know which town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten years that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste it. Including me, a bit. I'm good with lists but even I'd probably wait until year three. And the mine might not need me by then whether I'm ready or not.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people start now and that it's on workers, bosses and government together. I'd say that to anyone who asked.
S4.think: I think ten years is okay for me, because I'd have time to get good, get debt free and change track around thirty-two with savings. That's a normal career change.
S4.do: Clears debt, builds savings, then starts a night technical diploma in electrical work or automation once she sees what the mine hires for. Holds off on buying a home with her partner until she knows where they'll live.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but more like having homework than being afraid.
S4.quote: A little house with a shed in a town with a real supermarket.
S4.fieldNote: The decade makes her plan look like a normal career change, which reassures her. The cost lands on a quiet dream of a house of their own. She admits even she might waste the first years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd still have the debt when the job went, and that's the worst combination. What would help is help with debt, like a pause on loan payments for people who lose their jobs to this, and short courses that are free and lead to real jobs, not just certificates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like being a woman out here. It's fine now, mostly, but I fought to get in that seat. I'd hate the first time I'm finally good at something to be the year it stops mattering.

headlineQuote: I'd hate the first time I'm finally good at something to be the year it stops mattering.
portrait: Grace Evans is a 27-year-old junior excavator operator at a large lithium mine who came from a warehouse job for better pay and still carries a car loan and credit card debt. She lives with her partner Sam, who stacks supermarket shelves, uses AI apps now and then for admin, and copes with worry by making lists. Burned once by training for a job just before it was automated, she waits to see what works before she signs up for anything. The two-year picture alarms her because the debt would outlast the job, while ten years feels like an ordinary career change.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because she'd still have her debts when the job went.
whatWouldHelp: A pause on loan payments for people who lose work to automation, and free short courses that lead to real jobs.
